raw_response.country: Colombia, Italy, Tanzania, France, Argentina, and Canada

criterion_notes.c1: Examines urban drinking water supply (acueducto) and basic sanitation/sewerage (alcantarillado) service provision and household access across Colombia and selected international cities.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, the paper examines legal, constitutional, regulatory, and institutional reforms in the water sector (e.g., Colombia's 1991 Constitution, Law 142 of 1994, CRA regulation, privatization concessions, corporatization, and remunicipalisation). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, utility ownership and regulatory structure directly governing service access, tariff and cost-recovery rules, socioeconomic stratum subsidy caps, disconnection for non-payment, and minimum vital water allowances (Medellín Acuerdo 06 of 2011) are rule-type mechanisms directly governing service access.
criterion_notes.c3: No empirical evidence or systematic empirical synthesis (E05). The article has no Methods section, no primary quantitative or qualitative data collection, no original socio-legal empirical analysis, and no systematic review protocol; it is a narrative historical and policy overview compiling secondary literature, official/NGO reports, statutes, and newspaper articles.
criterion_notes.c4: Narratively cites secondary access-related figures from prior reports, including water and sewerage coverage rates, tariff increases, household disconnections for non-payment (e.g., in Medellín), and informalization of water access among low-income users in Cartagena.
criterion_notes.c5: Because the paper is an unstructured narrative overview without an empirical methodology, there is no identifiable empirical study design, sampling strategy, or analytical framework linking an exposure to an outcome.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in Spanish (with an English abstract). Per Criterion 10, assessment/translation directly from the provided Spanish full text is feasible by the screener; regardless of language, the paper is excluded under E05 for lacking empirical evidence.

evidence_quotes.quote: This article documents the public and private management water and basic sanitation service in some cities throughout the world.

Por esto, este articulo pretende documentar los casos de privatización del servicio de agua y saneamiento en ciudades urbanas y los casos de transición de algunas de ellas del manejo privado al público.

Debido a las particularidades de los servicios, la reglamentación conjunta ha tenido obstáculos para cumplirse de manera eficiente, un ejemplo de esto son los topes de subsidios para los ciudadanos por estratos que impiden la universalización de agua potable
Ello ha llevado, incluso, a que en Cartagena un sector cada vez más creciente de los usuarios más pobres se retiren de la provisión directa de los servicios de agua

Medellin fue la primera ciudad en contar con el programa mínimo Vital de Agua Potable que consiste en el descuento del valor de 2.5 metros cúbicos en el servicio de acueducto y alcantarillado por persona en el hogar

raw_response.exposure: Utility ownership and management regimes (privatization, concession/lease contracts, corporatization, and remunicipalisation) and regulatory/tariff frameworks (including Colombia's Law 142 of 1994, subsidy caps, and minimum vital water rules)
raw_response.outcome: Secondary descriptive indicators cited narratively from prior sources, including water and sewerage coverage, tariff levels, water losses, utility financial performance, and household disconnections for non-payment
raw_response.population_and_sample: Urban water supply and sanitation utilities/systems discussed narratively in Colombia (national historical trajectory, Cartagena, Medellín/EPM, Cali/EMCALI) and international case summaries (Italy, Dar es Salaam, Paris, Buenos Aires, Hamilton, Grenoble); no empirical sample reported
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). While the article addresses urban water and sanitation service access (c1) and discusses rule-type legal, ownership, regulatory, and tariff mechanisms under both the plain and narrow readings of Criterion 2 (c2), it is a non-empirical narrative historical and policy overview based entirely on secondary literature, reports, legislation, and press articles, with no empirical methods, no primary data, and no systematic synthesis design (c3=no, c5=no).
raw_response.study_design: Non-empirical narrative policy and historical overview (no empirical study design reported)
